strengths: Novel approach to MDM training acceleration by modifying the forward masking process to align training and inference distributions, orthogonal to architectural/recipe-level optimizations
Solid theoretical foundation with Proposition 1 (marginal agreement) and Proposition 2 (minimizer preservation) both carefully proven, providing clear intuition for why the method works
Practical efficiency: no forward-pass overhead, only one hyperparameter, compatible with other techniques (AR initialization, block diffusion)
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablations, robustness across multiple inference policies, and supporting evidence that unmasking policies stabilize early in training (Figures 3, 7)
Well-presented paper with clear motivation ('Train for the Worst'), good intuitive illustrations, complete algorithmic details (Algorithm 1), and honest discussion of limitations
Strong reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters (Table 1), pseudocode, multiple random seeds, and promised open-source release
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: primary evaluation only on TinyGSM (synthetic, structured corpus); no evaluation at larger scales (7B-100B mentioned in related work) or on real-world text corpora; authors acknowledge uncertainty about generalization to datasets with richer long-range dependencies

Material gap between claimed improvements: 2.5× iteration-accuracy speedup but only 1.1× wall-clock throughput gain (3.78 vs 3.41 it/s); authors attribute to 'implementation detail' but this undermines practical significance and deserves deeper investigation

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 1 assumes idealized single-position-per-step policy while practice uses evolved multi-position model policy; Proposition 3 sample complexity result applies only to toy distribution with restrictive assumptions; trajectory distance saturates at ~0.5 (Figure 7) with unexplored implications

K-scheduling appears critical but undermines core contribution: without it, performance is 1.9× slower (Figure 6); this suggests method requires careful tuning orthogonal to core teacher-forced chain idea
Effectiveness depends on inference flexibility: block diffusion reduces speedup to 1.7× (Figure 6), suggesting PUMA's benefit specifically requires unstructured inference order

Limited theoretical characterization: no systematic study of when train-test mismatch becomes problematic; Proposition 3 verification only on toy modular arithmetic example; missing analysis of failure modes

strengths: Sound theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs of marginal agreement (Prop 1) and minimizer preservation (Prop 2)
Clear and intuitive core idea: teacher-forced chains naturally align training and inference masking distributions
Thorough experimental methodology within scope: multiple seeds, ablations on hyperparameters, robustness across inference policies
Demonstrates complementarity with existing methods (ARM initialization, block diffusion)
No additional forward-pass computational overhead; clean implementation with provided pseudocode
Well-written presentation with good visualizations of the method and trajectory stabilization
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Severely limited experimental validation—only TinyGSM (synthetic structured code) and Sudoku, no real-world language datasets. Insufficient to assess generalization or practical impact for top-tier venue

CRITICAL: Wall-clock throughput improvement is only ~10% (3.41→3.78 it/s) despite 2.5× iteration speedup. The explanation (loss computation) is unsatisfying and undermines practical significance. This gap is not adequately addressed
CRITICAL: No comparison with other training acceleration methods (loss reweighting, block curriculum, etc.), making it impossible to assess relative efficiency or novelty of acceleration strategy

Theory-practice gap: Propositions assume fixed policy, but practice uses changing policy. Figure 7 shows trajectory distance saturates at 0.5, and no analysis of how policy nonstationarity affects guarantees
Method is sensitive and complex: K-scheduling is critical (Figure 6 shows 1.9× slowdown without it), confidence threshold requires tuning—contradicts 'simple modification' claim

Proposition 3 (sample complexity) proven only on artificial synthetic distribution with unvalidated assumptions; no empirical evidence that random masking actually causes exponential complexity in practice
Missing mechanistic understanding: Is speedup from masking alignment or other factors? What components are essential? Limited ablations isolating the policy alignment contribution
Scalability unknown: Only tested at 125M scale; unclear if wall-clock gaps persist/grow at larger scales, on diverse data, or in language generation tasks

strengths: Novel and elegant solution to well-motivated train-test mismatch problem in MDM training using teacher-forced chains that align training and inference masking distributions

Solid theoretical contributions with proper formal analysis: Proposition 1 (marginal agreement), Proposition 2 (minimizer preservation), and Proposition 3 (sample complexity separation between random and policy-guided masking)
Significant practical speedup of 2.5× on 125M models with zero forward-pass overhead, achieved through simple modification of forward process

Comprehensive experimental validation including ablations, robustness to different inference policies, compatibility with existing methods (ARM init, block diffusion), and Sudoku testbed that validates policy stabilization theory
Strong experimental practice: multiple seeds, detailed hyperparameters, thorough ablations showing K-scheduling and confidence thresholding are important, trajectory convergence analysis
Well-written and clearly structured paper with good visualizations (Figures 2-3 particularly effective) and transparent limitations discussion
Practical and orthogonal approach that compounds with other training acceleration techniques rather than replacing them
weaknesses: Empirical validation primarily limited to TinyGSM (synthetic, highly structured corpus); claims about generalization to natural language with richer dependencies are unvalidated, significantly limiting confidence in practical impact

Theoretical assumptions in Proposition 3 (posterior collapse, finite identifiability parameters) don't clearly map to natural language settings; connection between formal sample-complexity results and practical speedups is indirect

Practical interventions (K-scheduling, confidence thresholding) appear ad-hoc and lack theoretical justification; Figure 6 shows K-scheduling critical (1.9× *slower* without it), suggesting core idea needs these tweaks to work well

Modest wall-clock throughput gains (~11%) despite 2.5× iteration speedup; gap attributed to loss implementation details rather than algorithm, suggesting engineering overheads remain significant for practitioners

Policy stability assumption (current model's policy as proxy for final policy) validated only post-hoc empirically; theoretical guarantees don't cover early training with poor policies, and failure modes not discussed
Complementary speedup gains diminish substantially: 2.5× alone, 2.3× combined with ARM init, 1.7× with block diffusion, but this erosion with other methods not deeply analyzed
Limited sensitivity analysis: only 5 confidence thresholds tested (Figure 4-left), K-schedule appears highly tuned to TinyGSM, questions about when PUMA might hurt or fail remain unanswered

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated train-test mismatch problem in MDM training
Solid theoretical contributions with correct proofs for marginal agreement (Prop. 1) and minimizer preservation (Prop. 2)
Simple, practical method with no additional forward-pass overhead and straightforward implementation
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains with proper error bars and ablation studies
Demonstrates complementarity with other training techniques (ARM initialization showing 4.0× speedup, block diffusion)
Robust to different inference policies, showing generalization beyond the training policy
Good empirical insights (Figure 6) validating that policy ranking stabilizes early in training
Detailed algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) and complete hyperparameter tables aid reproducibility
weaknesses: Theory assumes fixed inference policy while practice uses the current model's policy, which changes during training—justified empirically but lacks formal guarantees
Limited to 125M pretraining and 7B post-training; no experiments at 70B+ scales where MDM training efficiency matters most for industry applications
Wall-clock throughput improvement (~1.1×) significantly lags iteration speedup (2.3×), with attribution to 'implementation details' that deserve deeper investigation
PUMA optimizes a different objective than NELBO (0.06 vs. 0.05 on TinyGSM), raising concerns for applications requiring principled variational bounds
Task-specific hyperparameter tuning (K-scheduling varies: 10 fixed for Sudoku, 42→12 for TinyGSM, 15 fixed for code) with limited guidance for new domains
Theory-practice gap partially masked by empirical validation; trajectory distance saturates at ~0.5 steps (Figure 6), indicating persistent policy divergence
Speedup degrades with more constrained inference (block size 256 gives only 1.7× vs. 2.3× for full model), limiting applicability in certain settings
Comparison to PAPL incomplete; doesn't explore when loss reweighting might be preferable or characterize the domains where each method excels

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated problem: train-test mismatch in MDM training where inference explores only a small fraction of masking patterns seen during random training
Theoretically solid with formal proofs: Proposition 1 establishes marginal agreement, Proposition 2 proves minimizer preservation, and Proposition 3 shows sample complexity separation
Elegant and simple core idea: teacher-forced chains are conceptually clean and easy to understand
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations across multiple datasets (Sudoku, TinyGSM, Dream-Coder) and demonstrated compatibility with other methods (ARM init, block diffusion)
Clear presentation with intuitive figures and well-structured writing
Shows empirical speedups of 2.3× at 125M scale and 4.0× with autoregressive initialization
Demonstrates robustness across different inference policies (Top-K, entropy-based, margin-based)
weaknesses: Critical gap: Main pretraining experiments limited to 125M scale; 7B experiments are fine-tuning only with LoRA, not full pretraining. For a scaling contribution, lack of validation at scales where MDMs actually matter (7B+) is a significant limitation
Wall-clock throughput degrades by 9% (3.78 vs 3.41 it/s) despite claims of 'no overhead.' Attribution to implementation details is hand-wavy; multiple samples per data point incurs real cost

NELBO results are concerning: vanilla MDM achieves lower NELBO (0.05 vs 0.06 on TinyGSM), the standard MDM objective. This raises fundamental questions about whether PUMA learns the correct distribution

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 1 assumes idealized policy unmasks one token per step; practice unmasks K tokens. Proposition 3 uses oracle trajectories; connection to actual PUMA (current model policy) never proven. Figure 6 shows trajectory distance saturates at 0.5, indicating persistent mismatch

Policy initialization circularity inadequately addressed: method depends on current noisy policy early in training. While Figure 6 suggests rapid convergence, saturation at 0.5 distance indicates never fully resolves
Proposition 2 not as special as claimed: forward process form (Eq. 2) with arbitrary weighting is satisfied by standard i.i.d. masking; minimizer preservation is not unique to PUMA

Limited comparison with related work: PAPL (addressing same problem) only compared in appendix; Self-Forcing mentioned but not empirically compared; claim that modifying forward process is 'substantially more effective than loss reweighting' not rigorously supported

Hyperparameter sensitivity and domain dependence: K-scheduling and confidence threshold require tuning; no systematic study of when PUMA helps vs. when it doesn't; PAPL results suggest performance depends on whether generation order matters

Practical interventions (confidence-based fast-forwarding, K-scheduling) feel ad-hoc rather than principled; Section 3.2.1 admits method 'need[s] two practical interventions,' suggesting core method insufficient

Sample efficiency not properly accounted for: each data point generates up to L/K training samples, effectively increasing sample complexity beyond what iteration-level speedup suggests; single-epoch limitation downplayed
Reproducibility concerns: code promised but not provided; streaming buffer implementation complex and error-prone; details scattered throughout appendix

strengths: Sound theoretical foundation with formal propositions proving marginal agreement, minimizer preservation, and sample complexity benefits; proofs are rigorous and elegant
Novel approach to an underexplored problem: identifies and addresses the train-test mismatch in MDMs through forward process modification rather than inference or recipes
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (Sudoku, code, math) with proper methodology: 3 seeds, 95% CIs, and consistent speedups (1.7-4.0×)
Complementary to existing techniques: demonstrates 4.0× combined speedup with ARM initialization and compatibility with block diffusion
Practical implementation: streaming teacher-forced chains with negligible computational overhead and clear algorithmic description

Excellent presentation: well-motivated problem statement, clear figures (particularly Figure 2 and 3), comprehensive appendix, and insightful broader perspective on discrete vs. continuous diffusion design spaces
Robustness across inference policies: single PUMA-trained model generalizes to multiple unmasking strategies, crucial for practical deployment
Thorough ablations: K-scheduling, confidence thresholds, and inference policies systematically studied
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: assumes final inference policy during training but uses current model's policy; while argued reasonable, Figure 6 shows trajectory distance saturates at ~0.5, indicating imperfect alignment even on Sudoku

Limited experimental scale: main pretraining at 125M (small by 2025 standards); post-training uses LoRA with 300M parameters; no experiments at 13B-100B scales where MDMs are most relevant for production
Wall-clock throughput regression: PUMA runs 9.8% slower per iteration (3.41 vs 3.78 it/s); speedup claims are iteration-accuracy rather than wall-clock time, limiting practical impact

NELBO concerns: vanilla MDM achieves lower NELBO on TinyGSM (0.05 vs 0.06); while explained, raises questions about whether PUMA optimizes the correct objective, particularly important for RL applications
Incomplete PAPL comparison: surprising that loss reweighting fails while distribution modification succeeds; detailed comparison relegated to appendix despite both addressing train-test mismatch

Single-epoch training limitation: PUMA requires multiple forward passes per sample, making it inefficient in memory-constrained single-epoch setups; comparison at equal gradient steps is somewhat indirect

Sample complexity analysis (Proposition 3) uses artificial toy distribution (additive group mod m); connection between oracle trajectories and PUMA's actual trajectories unclear; applicability to complex real distributions limited

Practical interventions move from theory: K-scheduling and confidence-based fast-forwarding improve efficiency but diverge from the idealized theoretical setup, creating an unquantified theory-practice gap
